title: Apple's Foldable iPhone: Will the Ultra Finally Make the Fold Worth It?
summary: Apple is rumored to be finally entering the foldable smartphone market with its "iPhone Ultra," a move that follows nearly a decade of development by competitors. The key question remains whether Apple's late entry will deliver groundbreaking innovation and justify its inevitable premium price.
content:
The whisper campaign has turned into a roar: Apple is finally poised to enter the foldable smartphone arena. For years, tech enthusiasts have debated when (not if) the Cupertino giant would embrace the form factor that rivals like Samsung, Oppo, and Honor have been meticulously refining for nearly a decade. This rumored device, potentially dubbed the iPhone Ultra, isn't just another iPhone; it represents Apple's long-anticipated foray into a market ripe with both innovation and pitfalls.

Apple’s modus operandi has always been to observe, learn, and then perfect. While other manufacturers wrestled with creased screens, durability concerns, and software quirks in the early days, Apple bided its time. The expectation now is that an iPhone Ultra Fold won't merely replicate existing designs but will arrive with Apple’s signature polish: seamless hardware-software integration, robust build quality, and an intuitive user experience that justifies its inevitable premium price tag.

But here’s the million-dollar question: will it be *worth* the money? The foldable market, though maturing, still caters to a niche willing to pay for cutting-edge tech. Apple will need to offer more than just a folding screen. It must deliver a compelling reason for consumers to abandon their traditional iPhones or existing foldables, perhaps through groundbreaking hinge technology, unparalleled display resilience, or revolutionary software features that truly leverage the dual-screen form factor. Simply put, Apple can't just be *late*; it needs to be *better*.

The potential arrival of an iPhone Ultra Fold marks a pivotal moment for both Apple and the broader smartphone industry. Its success, or lack thereof, will undoubtedly reshape expectations for future foldable innovations. The world waits to see if Apple's patience will pay off, delivering a foldable that genuinely redefines the category, or if it will be seen as a costly catch-up in an already competitive race.
keyTakeaways: Apple is widely rumored to be entering the foldable smartphone market with a device potentially named the iPhone Ultra.
Apple's entry comes nearly a decade after competitors like Samsung, raising questions about its innovation and value proposition.
The success of the iPhone Ultra Fold will depend on its ability to deliver superior hardware-software integration and justify its premium price tag.
author: Roland Hutchinson

title: Shadow IT Gets an AI Upgrade: Why Your Enterprise is More Vulnerable Than Ever
summary: Artificial intelligence, while boosting innovation, has inadvertently created a massive cybersecurity blind spot by enabling employees to easily deploy internet-facing applications outside of traditional security protocols. This unchecked proliferation of unknown and unmanaged assets dramatically expands an organization's attack surface, exposing them to heightened risk of breaches and compliance failures.
content:
Artificial intelligence has rapidly become the accelerant of our era, pushing innovation at breakneck speed across every industry imaginable. From automating complex tasks to powering groundbreaking business models, AI's transformative impact is undeniable. Yet, amidst this technological surge, a critical, often overlooked, vulnerability is rapidly expanding within enterprise security perimeters, threatening to undo much of the progress.

The very tools that empower rapid development and deployment, particularly low-code/no-code platforms infused with generative AI capabilities, are inadvertently fostering a dangerous new iteration of "shadow IT." Departments and even individual employees can now effortlessly spin up internet-facing applications without the traditional oversight of central security teams. This ease of deployment, while beneficial for agility, routinely bypasses established security gates, creating an ever-growing array of unmanaged digital assets exposed to the public internet.

Rob Gurzeev, CEO of cybersecurity firm CyCognito, points to this phenomenon as a significant and escalating blind spot for organizations. "AI makes it trivially easy for anyone in an organization to deploy internet-facing applications, often outside established security processes," Gurzeev explains. The consequence? A vast, uncharted territory of forgotten, misconfigured, or simply unknown assets — each a potential entry point for malicious actors.

This unchecked proliferation means organizations are struggling to identify, inventory, and secure everything that exists on their external attack surface. It's a game of whack-a-mole where new vulnerabilities appear faster than security teams can even spot them, let alone address them. The stakes are immense: undetected flaws can lead to devastating data breaches, severe compliance violations, and irreversible reputational damage.

As AI continues to democratize software creation and deployment, the immediate challenge for cybersecurity leaders isn't just about protecting known assets, but about achieving comprehensive, real-time visibility into a constantly evolving and expanding digital frontier. The race is on to illuminate these newly formed blind spots before they become the next major headlines.
keyTakeaways: AI tools enable non-security personnel to easily deploy internet-facing applications, often bypassing established security processes.
This creates a rapidly expanding 'blind spot' of unmanaged and unknown digital assets within organizations' external attack surfaces.
The unchecked proliferation of these unmonitored assets significantly increases enterprise vulnerability to cyber threats and data breaches.
author: Kolawole Samuel Adebayo

title: GE's GEnx-1B Engines Soar Past 50 Million Flight Hours, Setting a Blazing New Record
summary: GE Aerospace's GEnx-1B engine recently shattered a company record, accumulating an astounding 50 million flight hours in just over 14 years. This unprecedented pace marks it as the fastest widebody engine model in GE's history to reach such a significant operational milestone, underscoring its pivotal role in modern aviation.
content:
FARNBOROUGH, England – In a stunning testament to modern aerospace engineering and relentless reliability, GE Aerospace announced today that its GEnx-1B engine has officially surpassed the monumental 50 million flight hour mark. What makes this achievement truly remarkable is the speed at which it was reached: a mere 14 years since its entry into service, making it the fastest widebody engine model in GE’s storied history to hit such a significant milestone.

This isn't just a number; it's a testament to the workhorse of the skies. The GEnx-1B, a powerhouse specifically designed for the Boeing 787 Dreamliner and the 747-8, has quietly become the cornerstone of long-haul passenger and cargo flights worldwide. Its rapid accumulation of flight hours speaks volumes about its omnipresence in the global fleet and the trust airlines place in its performance day in and day out.

The 50 million hour threshold isn't merely an operational metric; it’s a living, breathing proof point of the engine’s design prowess and its impact on the aviation industry. Airlines benefit from its renowned fuel efficiency, a critical factor in today's economic climate, while passengers enjoy quieter cabins and fewer delays thanks to its robust reliability. This milestone underscores not only GE Aerospace's engineering excellence but also the GEnx-1B's enduring legacy in shaping the landscape of modern air travel.

As the engines continue to power flights across continents, this record-breaking pace solidifies the GEnx-1B's position as a titan of the skies, consistently delivering on the promise of efficient, dependable air transport for millions.
keyTakeaways: The GE Aerospace GEnx-1B engine has accumulated over 50 million flight hours.
It reached this milestone in just over 14 years, marking it as the fastest widebody engine in GE's history to do so.
The GEnx-1B powers the Boeing 787 Dreamliner and 747-8, highlighting its critical role in global aviation.
author: GE Aerospace
